group.title: Study and learning
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: A place where people study for a degree after school.
wrong: Children start university when they are five.

words.meaning: To finish a course at a university or school successfully.
examples: He {graduated} in 2020 with a degree in history.
wrong: She graduated, so she never finished her course.

words.meaning: A talk to a group of students about a subject.
examples: The {lecture} on climate starts at nine.
wrong: A lecture is a short chat between two friends on the bus.

words.meaning: One of the two parts of a school or university year.
examples: Exams are at the end of the {semester}.
wrong: A semester lasts for one afternoon.

words.meaning: A short piece of writing on one subject.
examples: I have to write an {essay} about my hometown.
wrong: An essay is a kind of exam you answer by singing.

words.meaning: A piece of work a student is given to do.
wrong: An assignment is work that nobody asks you to do.

words.meaning: A letter or number that shows how good a student’s work is.
examples: She got a good {grade} in math.
wrong: My grade is the name of my teacher.

words.meaning: An official paper that shows you have done a course.
examples: You’ll get a {certificate} at the end of the course.
wrong: A certificate is a kind of exam that you fail.

words.meaning: Money given to a student to pay for their studies.
examples: She won a {scholarship} to study abroad.
wrong: A scholarship is money a student pays to the teacher as a fine.

words.meaning: To study again what you have learned, before an exam.
examples: I need to {revise} for my history test.
wrong: I revised for the exam by forgetting everything.

words.meaning: To learn something so you can remember it exactly.
wrong: I memorized the poem, so I can’t remember a word of it.

words.meaning: The information and understanding you have.
examples: He has a good {knowledge} of music.
wrong: Knowledge is the money you keep in a bank.

words.meaning: To give all your attention to something.
wrong: I concentrated on the book by looking out of the window.

words.meaning: To go to an event, school or meeting.
wrong: I attended the meeting by staying at home and ignoring it.

words.meaning: To not pass a test or exam.
wrong: She failed the exam with the highest grade.

words.meaning: To be successful in a test or exam.
wrong: He passed the test because all his answers were wrong.

words.meaning: To act in a dishonest way to get an advantage, for example in a test.
examples: Anyone who {cheats} will fail the exam.
wrong: She cheated by working honestly on her own.

words.meaning: Not at a place where you should be.
wrong: He was absent, so he sat in the front row.

words.meaning: A talk that shows and explains something to a group.
wrong: A presentation is a gift you open on your birthday.

words.meaning: A talk between people about a subject.
examples: We had a {discussion} about the plan.
wrong: We had a discussion, but nobody said a word.

words.meaning: A senior teacher at a university.
wrong: A professor is a child in the first year of school.

words.meaning: A teacher who teaches one student or a small group.
wrong: A tutor is a student who never helps anyone.

words.meaning: A set of classes on a subject.
wrong: A course is a single minute of a lesson.

words.meaning: A book used for studying a subject.
wrong: A textbook is a book of jokes for fun.

words.meaning: The land and buildings of a university.
examples: The library is in the middle of the {campus}.
wrong: A campus is a small shop in the city.

words.meaning: To officially join a course or school.
wrong: I enrolled in the course, so I’m not a student.

words.meaning: A paper that shows you have finished a course of study.
wrong: A diploma is the ticket you need for a train.

words.meaning: To give someone confidence or support to do something.
examples: My parents {encouraged} me to study music.
wrong: He encouraged me by telling me to give up.

words.meaning: The wish to do something.
examples: She has a lot of {motivation} to learn.
wrong: He has no motivation, so he wants to work hard.

words.meaning: Hard work done to try to do something.
examples: He made a big {effort} to learn Spanish.
wrong: She passed with great effort, so it was very easy.

words.meaning: Something that is wrong or not correct.
examples: There are two {mistakes} in your letter.
wrong: A mistake is an answer that is completely correct.

words.meaning: Movement toward a better level.
wrong: I made progress, so I got worse.

words.meaning: To succeed in doing something after effort.
examples: She {achieved} her goal of running a marathon.
wrong: He achieved his goal by never trying.

words.meaning: A short informal test.
examples: We have a vocabulary {quiz} every Friday.
wrong: A quiz is a long book you read for fun.

words.meaning: Information that tells you how to do something.
wrong: The instructions told us nothing about how to do it.

words.meaning: Words that make something clear.
wrong: His explanation made the problem harder to understand.

words.meaning: Something that shows what other things of the same kind are like.
wrong: An example is a rule that has no cases.

words.meaning: To change words into another language.
wrong: I translated it, so it stayed in the same language.

words.meaning: All the words of a language, or the words a person knows.
wrong: Vocabulary is the grammar of numbers.

words.meaning: To make the sound of a word.
wrong: I pronounce the word by writing it down.
